stated_availability: Descriptive only (not mapped to L1-L6). The paper carries no data availability statement. The sole deposit statement is back matter: "Appendix A. Supplementary data — Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921." Code availability is stated twice in the Methods: "All analyses were undertaken in 'R' version 4.3.0. The script used to run all validation analyses is available in the supplementary information." (Section 2.3.3) and "The script used to run all case study tests is available in the supplementary information." (Section 2.4). The supplement is described as containing scripts plus Supplementary Tables 1-3 and Supplementary Figs. 1-3 (result tables/figures); no data files are ever mentioned. Article is gold open access: "0305-4403/© 2023 The Authors. This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)." No repository, no dataset DOI/accession, no ORCIDs printed, no embargo or ethical-restriction statement.

F1.evidence: No dataset DOI, accession, or repository identifier appears anywhere in the paper. The only persistent identifier present is the article DOI (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921), and the sole deposit statement, 'Appendix A. Supplementary data', is described in the Methods as holding scripts ('The script used to run all case study tests is available in the supplementary information'), never data files. Per the guide, 'Only URLs or available on request -> 0 points'; here not even a URL for data exists.

F2.evidence: No structured metadata record (creators, title, keywords, description, format, size) exists for any of the 12 morphometric datasets. They are described only in narrative Methods prose (Section 2.4) and as summary statistics: Table 1 reports 'Mean, SD, CV, Minimum, Maximum' for the two replica assemblages. No repository metadata, no data dictionary.

F3.evidence: No data identifier exists (F1 = 0), so no metadata record can explicitly include it. The paper's own text links datasets to source publications by citation only (e.g., 'The methods used to collect these morphometric data are described in Key and Lycett (2017)'), not by dataset PID.

F4.evidence: No data are registered or indexed in any searchable resource. No Zenodo, Figshare, Dryad, tDAR, Open Context, ARIADNEplus, or institutional repository is named anywhere in the article; the only hosting mentioned is the publisher supplement attached to the article DOI.

A1.evidence: Completeness rule triggered: data_completeness coverage_category = 'minimal' (2/12 datasets at Tier 0-2 = 16.7%), so A1 = 0 for data FAIR. Independently, no record-level morphometric data are retrievable by any protocol from this paper: values appear only as aggregate statistics in Tables 1-7. No ethical or legal restriction is claimed anywhere, so the CARE/ethics exception does not apply — the paper states only that 'In all cases, morphometric data were collected prior to the present study being conceived.'

A1_1.evidence: There is no accessible data resource whose retrieval protocol could be assessed. The only openly available representation of the research data is summary statistics inside the PDF (Tables 1, 5, 6, 7), which the FAIR guide classes as not machine-actionable ('PDF supplementary materials with data tables ... requires manual transcription').

A1_2.evidence: No authentication or authorisation procedure is documented, and no ethical, legal, or CARE-based justification is offered for withholding the data — the paper carries no data availability statement at all. This is the guide's 'completely closed with no justification -> 0 points' case rather than a governed-restriction positive signal.

A2.evidence: No dataset metadata record exists that could persist independently of the data (no repository landing page, no tombstone, no DataCite/registry entry). Nothing beyond narrative Methods prose would remain if the underlying measurements were lost.

I1.evidence: No formal, machine-parseable knowledge representation is used for the data: no CSV/JSON/XML deposit is described. The only public representation is PDF tables of descriptive statistics and OLE estimates (Tables 1-7), which the guide scores 0 ('Unstructured format (PDF tables, Word doc, scanned images, plain text) -> 0 points').

I2.evidence: No controlled vocabulary, ontology, or standardised term set is applied to the morphometric variables. Field names are ad hoc measurement labels defined in table captions ('Length, breadth, and thickness values are in millimetres (mm), while mass is in grams (g)'); no PeriodO, Getty AAT, CIDOC-CRM, or ARIADNEplus vocabulary is cited.

I3.evidence: No qualified, typed references link a data resource to other resources via PIDs. Relationships between the study's data and prior work exist only as bibliographic citations in running text (e.g., 'Data are derived from Buchanan and Hamilton's (2021) study of scaling laws in Paleoindian points'), which are untyped and not attached to any released data object.

R1.evidence: No released data resource exists to be richly described. The paper does describe the underlying assemblages in prose (site, chronology, sample size, variables — e.g., 'we limit the present case study to the whole flakes excavated from MIS 15 sediments in the 2020 season (n = 173)'), but these descriptions attach to unreleased, non-retrievable data; the instrument scores evidenced practice for the artefact.

R1_1.evidence: No data usage licence is stated for any dataset. The CC BY 4.0 statement on page 1 ('This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)') covers the article and its appendices, but no data artefact is released for it to apply to, and no dataset-level licence, terms of reuse, or SPDX identifier appears.

R1_2.evidence: No provenance metadata is associated with any data resource, because none is released. Provenance information does exist in prose for each case study (collector, curation location, and method citations — e.g., the replica Early Archaic points were 'originally knapped by M.I.E. in 2021' and 'have since been curated at the Kent State University Experimental Archaeology Laboratory'), but it is not attached to a retrievable dataset or metadata record.

R1_3.evidence: No domain-relevant data standard is applied or claimed (no Dublin Core, DataCite, ARIADNEplus, tDAR, or Open Context conformance). Measurement protocols follow discipline conventions by citation (e.g., 'following the method outlined by de la Peña and Wadley (2014)'), but that is protocol practice, not a data-standards conformance statement for a deposited dataset.

F1.evidence: The scripts are retrievable through a persistent, resolvable DOI: 'The script used to run all validation analyses is available in the supplementary information' (Section 2.3.3) and 'The script used to run all case study tests is available in the supplementary information' (Section 2.4), with 'Appendix A. Supplementary data — Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921.' Caveat recorded: this is the article-level Crossref DOI, not a code-specific DOI, SWHID, or Zenodo archive; no software PID is issued.

F2.evidence: No metadata record describes the code. The paper gives no script filename, title, version, author attribution, dependency list, or description beyond the one-line availability sentences; no CITATION.cff, codemeta.json, or README is mentioned. This is the guide's 'just a file with filename only -> 0 points' case (indeed, not even a filename).

F3.evidence: There is no code-level metadata record, so no metadata explicitly carries the identifier of the software it describes. The DOI printed in Appendix A identifies the article, and no software metadata is bound to it.

F4.evidence: The code is not registered or indexed in any searchable software resource: no CRAN, Zenodo, Software Heritage, GitHub, JOSS, or institutional repository is named. It exists only as an undifferentiated publisher supplement attached to the article record.

A1.evidence: The code is retrievable by DOI resolution over HTTPS from the publisher: 'Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921.' Coverage of the analyses appears complete — separate scripts are stated to run 'all validation analyses' and 'all case study tests'.

A1_1.evidence: Retrieval is via open, free, universally implementable HTTPS/DOI resolution with no subscription or login barrier: the article is gold open access ('0305-4403/© 2023 The Authors. This is an open access article under the CC BY license'), so its supplementary files are publicly downloadable.

A1_2.evidence: Access is open by default over HTTPS, a protocol that supports authentication and authorisation where necessary; no restriction applies to these scripts and none is needed. This is not the guide's 'completely closed with no justification' case.

A2.evidence: No metadata record or preservation commitment is evidenced for the code artefact itself. No repository with a metadata-persistence guarantee (Zenodo, DANS, Software Heritage) is used, and no tombstone/registry entry would describe the scripts if the supplementary file became unavailable — only the one-line in-text sentences would remain.

I1.evidence: The code is plain R source in a formal, open, broadly applicable language, with the runtime named: 'All analyses were undertaken in R version 4.3.0.' This matches the guide's precedent of awarding I1 for 'standard format - Python/R code'.

I2.evidence: No vocabularies, schemas, or machine-readable dependency declarations that themselves follow FAIR principles are used or cited: no codemeta/JSON-LD, no DESCRIPTION/renv.lock, and no R packages are named anywhere in the article.

I3.evidence: No qualified, PID-typed references link the code to its inputs or dependencies. The scripts' data inputs are described only bibliographically in the Methods (e.g., 'Data are derived from Buchanan and Hamilton's (2021) study'), and no data DOI, software DOI, or typed relation ('is derived from', 'uses software') is provided.

R1.evidence: The analyses the scripts implement are described in reproducible detail in the Methods: 'we ... use the 10 (k) largest or smallest measurements of a given trait', 'we also assessed the use of k values of 5, 20 and 30 for all validation tests', subsampling 'at rates of 5%, 10%, 20%, and 50% relative to the total number of records', 'One thousand iterations of each process were performed', the duplicate-resampling procedure (Section 2.4.1.6.1), and the runtime 'R version 4.3.0'. This satisfies the guide's 'methods description' route to R1, although no README or in-repository documentation is evidenced.

R1_1.evidence: A clear, accessible, SPDX-mappable licence is printed on the article and covers the article including its Appendix A supplementary data: '0305-4403/© 2023 The Authors. This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)' (CC-BY-4.0). Caveat recorded: no code-specific licence file or software licence (MIT/GPL/Apache) is attached to the scripts themselves.

R1_2.evidence: Provenance for the code artefact is not detailed: no version number, release date, commit history, package/dependency versions, or random seeds are documented, and the CRediT statement assigns no 'Software' role to any author (e.g., 'Alastair Key: Conceptualization, Data curation, Formal analysis, Investigation, Methodology, Validation, Writing - original draft, Writing - review & editing'), so script authorship is unattributed. The single R version (4.3.0) falls short of 'detailed provenance'.

R1_3.evidence: No domain or software community standard is applied: no research compendium/rrtools structure, no CRAN packaging, no CITATION.cff or codemeta.json, no container or environment specification, and no conformance statement. Sharing is an undocumented script bundled as a journal supplement.

barriers: No data availability statement anywhere in the article; the only deposit (Appendix A) is described as containing analysis scripts and supplementary tables/figures, never data files

Co-author-held, undeposited assemblage data: replica Acheulean handaxes (n = 500), replica Early Archaic points (n = 45, 'curated at the Kent State University Experimental Archaeology Laboratory', from an experiment that 'never came to fruition'), copper socketed tang points (n = 93, no data source cited at all)
Unpublished PhD thesis as sole source for the Olduvai Bed III/IV cleaver data (Martín-Ramos, C., 2022 ... 'Unpublished PhD thesis. University College London')
Closed monographs as sources for both ceramic case studies (Petrie 2020, Oxbow Books, Bannu Basin bowls n = 1466; Robb 2007, Cambridge University Press, Neolithic Impressed Ware and Stentinello pots)

Paywalled journal articles cited for measurement *methods* rather than for data (Key and Lycett 2017; de la Peña and Wadley 2014; Cortell-Nicolau et al. 2023; Proffitt et al. 2016), so retrieval of record-level values is not enabled
Record-level measurements appear publicly only as aggregate statistics in PDF tables (Tables 1, 5, 6, 7), which are not machine-actionable

Third-party availability at the two Tier 2 sources (Key et al. 2022, R. Soc. Open Sci.; Buchanan and Hamilton 2021, Sci. Rep. — both open-access venues with data-availability mandates) could not be verified from the paper alone; classified Tier 2 on the generous side, and the coverage category is 'minimal' under either treatment
